grammarDeepDive: The present perfect is the tense of achievements and results — it connects past actions to the present: 'IT has improved efficiency across all departments' , 'The team has reduced downtime by 40%' . title: Managing Software Portfolios
objective: Manage a company's software portfolio actively, not reactively.
grammarDetail: Passive with modal verbs. Example: Every tool must be owned. The portfolio should be reviewed every six months.
grammarDeepDive: Managing a software portfolio means talking about quantities: 'There are too many applications' , 'We have enough tools' , ' Several departments share the same CRM' . Quantifiers help you describe amounts precisely — essential for budget discussions, audits and resource planning. Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar explains: too many/too much = more than needed (negative), enough = the right amount (positive), several = more than two but not very many. Murphy's Grammar in Use adds: too many + countable plural ( 'too many apps' ), too much + uncountable ( 'too much software' ). title: Working with IT Teams Effectively

grammarDetail: Complex sentences.  Because, so, although. Example: We asked IT for an outcome, so they suggested a simpler solution we had not thought of.
grammarDeepDive: Business English is full of phrasal verbs — two-word verbs that have a special meaning: ' Set up a meeting' , ' Roll out the new system' , ' Follow up on the ticket' . In IT collaboration, these phrasal verbs are used daily and understanding them is essential for clear communication with technical teams. grammarDeepDive: When choosing between infrastructure options, expressing preference clearly is essential: 'Czarnikow prefers cloud for collaboration' , 'We would rather adopt a hybrid approach' , ' Instead of migrating everything, we move workloads gradually' . These structures help you articulate choices diplomatically and clearly. Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar explains three main preference structures: prefer + noun/-ing ( 'prefer cloud' ), would rather + base verb ( 'would rather use cloud' ), and instead of + noun/-ing ( 'instead of buying servers' ). title: Managing Networks and Connectivity
objective: Manage network and connectivity issues calmly at the intermediate level.
grammarDetail: Present perfect continuous. Example: The Wi-Fi has been getting slower for weeks. Users have been mentioning it quietly.
grammarDeepDive: In network management, you often report what others have said: 'The CTO said that bandwidth had increased' , 'IT told us that the firewall would be upgraded' . Reported speech transforms direct quotes into indirect reports — essential for meeting minutes, status updates and incident documentation. The main rule is backshift : present → past, past → past perfect, will → would. Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar provides full backshift tables. Murphy's Grammar in Use explains: 'The network is fine' → 'IT said the network was fine' ; 'We will upgrade' → 'IT said they would upgrade' . title: Data Storage and Backup Strategy

grammarDetail: Modal verbs for strategy.  Should, must, ought to. Example: We should test restores every month. Backups must exist in two different types of storage.
grammarDeepDive: The second conditional describes hypothetical or unlikely situations: 'If we had a better backup system, we would recover faster' . Unlike the first conditional (real possibility), the second conditional imagines situations that are not currently true — perfect for discussing improvements, what-if scenarios and strategic planning. The structure is: If + past simple, would + base verb . Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar calls this the 'unreal conditional' because the if-clause describes something contrary to reality. title: Understanding AI in Practice
objective: Understand what AI can and cannot do in a real business setting.
grammarDetail: Linking words.  Because, so, although. Example: AI is good at patterns, so it helps with summarisation, although it struggles with real-world judgement.
grammarDeepDive: When discussing AI capabilities, can and could express what is possible: 'AI can analyse thousands of data points in seconds' (present ability), 'Machine learning could predict market trends' (theoretical possibility). The choice between them signals certainty: can = it definitely does this; could = it might, under the right conditions. Eastwood's Oxford Practice Grammar explains: can = present ability or general possibility, could = conditional possibility or past ability. Murphy's Grammar in Use adds: can't/cannot = impossibility: 'AI cannot replace human judgement' . For polite or tentative suggestions, 'could' is softer: 'AI could help optimise logistics' (a suggestion, not a certainty).
